newsitem.title: UK: Lonrho break-up to end conflict-ridden era.
newsitem.headline: Lonrho break-up to end conflict-ridden era.

text.p: A three-year tale of board room rows, personality clashes and strategy changes at Lonrho is reaching its final chapter with chief Dieter Bock's decision to step down ahead of the conglomerate's imminent break-up.
The split, devised by Bock, will mark the end of three decades of empire building by founder Tiny Rowland, ousted in March last year after a series of bitter power struggles.

Lonrho's grand finale was announced on Tuesday when Bock sold all his shares for 257 million pounds ($416.9 million) to South African powerhouse Anglo American, which is eyeing the conglomerate's huge mining interests.
At the same time, Lonrho said it is about to conclude the sale of its hotel chains, which is to be followed by the divestment of the African trading operations, in which Bock wants to hold a stake.
The German property dealer, who will continue as non-executive deputy chairman, said he wants to step out of the limelight to avoid conflict of interests while Lonrho's long-muted split takes place.
Commenting on the latest developments, business tycoon Rowland told Reuters: "It is all fine for Anglo, but it's bad news for Lonrho shareholders."
Industry watchers, however, have been supporters of the break-up, even though Lonrho's shares have languished in line with other conglomerates since the split was announced in February.
"The break-up is necessary to create value for shareholders," said Charles Kernot at Paribas Capital Markets.
Analysts believe the unbundling became necessary as Lonrho had developed into a non-transparent web of over 500 firms.

Lonrho's main assets are its mining operations, valued at about one billion pounds. The business includes coal and platinum activities in South Africa and a stake of about 30 percent in Ghana's Ashanti Goldfields.
Anglo American, which now holds 25.9 percent, is believed to be particularly interested in forging a link with Ashanti, which is one of the world biggest gold mines.
Analysts said that Anglo American now effectively controls a 30 percent stake in Ashanti through its Lonrho holding.

But industry sources told Reuters earlier this week that the Ghanaian government wants to keep the giant South African company at bay, fearing a link may harm Ashanti's good relations with other African countries.

Bock, who joined Lonrho in 1993, initially wanted to demerge the mining interests as a separately listed company, but changed course this summer when he announced plans to float off the hotels instead.

That plan was consequently dropped last month as several potential buyers emerged for Lonrho's five Metropole hotels in Britain as well as the Princess chain, which includes 10 hotels in the Caribbean, Mexico and the U.S.
The two chains have an estimated total worth of about 700 million pounds.
Britain's Stakis has been frequently rumoured to be interested in Metropole, while Saudi Prince al-Waleed bibn Talal hasd been mentioned as a potential buyer of the Princess hotels.
The rest of Lonrho mainly consists of a wide variety of trading operations mainly located in Africa and valued at about 780 million pounds.
It is still unclear whether these activities will be spun off through an outright sale or via a demerger, which is preferred by analysts.
"If there is a demerger investors can retain full exposure to Africa, rather than being left with just a holding in a mining firm controlled by Anglo," said Kernot.
Lonrho shares were down 5-1/2 pence at 158 pence by 1345 GMTin early afternoon trade. ($1=.6165 Pound)
